chapter_theme: The invocation and the first twenty verses each count four painful things, setting failures of worship, kingship, friendship, learning and the household beside plain images of things without their ground (a scentless flower, an unfenced cane field, a weapon in weak hands), so that a fault of conduct is read as one more thing cut off from what makes it work.

0.reading: The invocation counts four things as painful, all failures of worship: not worshipping the feet of the three-eyed Lord, living without thinking of the white god of the golden palmyra, forgetting the one who bears the discus, and not worshipping the feet of the one who bears the spear.
0.nuance: The four gods are named by emblems only: three eyes (Siva), the golden palmyra banner and white colour (most likely Balarama), the discus (Vishnu) and the சத்தி spear (most likely Murugan). The dative தார்க்கு puts the pain on the one who neglects worship, so the book opens by counting a lack in the person, as its verses go on to do.

items.claim: not worshipping the feet of the three-eyed Lord is painful to the one who neglects it
living without keeping in mind the white god of the golden palmyra is painful
forgetting the god who bears the discus is painful
not worshipping the feet of the spear-bearer is painful to the one who neglects it

1.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the beauty of a house that has no tie of kin, the good looks of a son who has no father, eating while staying in the house of brahmins, and a mantra that does not take effect.
1.nuance: The first two items are beauty without the bond that should frame it (a house without kin, a son without a father). The third is unclear: the verse does not say whose pain it is, the outsider eating in a brahmin house or the brahmins whose house is used, and Project Madurai's variant ஊணின்னாது would make it 'not painful'. மந்திரம் may be a ritual formula or a counsel; வாயா விடின் says only that it does not come off.

items.claim: beauty in a house with no tie of kin is painful
the good looks of a son who has no father are painful
eating while lodging in the house of brahmins is counted painful, for an unstated party
a mantra that does not take effect is painful

norm.note: a rule of the period about eating in a brahmin's house and about the efficacy of mantra, stated without saying who is barred

2.reading: The verse counts four painful things: a fowl and a dog entering a brahmin's house, the unruliness of a wedded wife, wearing a garment that lacks its proper பாத்து, and the land of a king who does not protect it.
2.nuance: The first item is a pollution and birth rule: பார்ப்பார் names brahmins as a birth group, and the fowl and the dog are counted as defiling their house. The second makes a wife's lack of restraint (அடங்காமை) a pain for the house, a gender norm of the period. The third line is corrupt (புநடைவை, likely for புடைவை), and பாத்து may mean a border or one's own share, so the item cannot be fixed.

items.claim: a fowl and a dog entering a brahmin's house is counted painful
the unruliness of the wife one has bound in marriage is very painful
wearing a garment without its பாத்து is painful (sense uncertain)
the land of a king who does not protect it is painful

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period (animals defiling a brahmin household) beside a norm of the wife's restraint

3.reading: The verse counts four painful things: living under fierce kings of bent sceptre, swimming long water without a float, association with men of harsh speech, and living in wavering confusion.
3.nuance: The second item is the image for the rest: under a cruel king, among harsh speakers or in an unsettled mind, one is in deep water with nothing to hold. The last item names its sufferer, உயிர்க்கு, so wavering is a pain to life itself.

items.claim: living as a subject under fierce kings of bent sceptre is painful
swimming deep water without a float is painful
close association with men of harsh speech is painful
living in wavering confusion is painful to one's very life

4.reading: The verse counts four painful things: for ploughmen without oxen, the wet of the soil passing unused; turning one's back in battle with weapons lost; provoking those who have fortune; and doing harm to the very strong.
4.nuance: The first item is a matter of timing: the soil's moisture (ஈரம்) goes by while the ox-less farmer cannot plough. The last two are prudential: the pain is the one the provoker brings on himself. கருவிகண் in line 2 may be கருவிகள் misprinted, or 'where weapons are exchanged'.

items.claim: for ploughmen without oxen, the soil's moisture passing unused is painful
turning one's back in battle with weapons changed or lost is painful
provoking those who have fortune is painful
doing harm to the very strong is painful

5.reading: The verse counts four painful things: guarding sugarcane that has no fence, living under an old roof that lets the rain drip through, a kingship that rules without justice, and a deed done without secrecy.
5.nuance: The two images of unprotected keeping (cane without a fence, a house without a sound roof) come before the two cases they illuminate: rule without முறை and action without மறை. The pairing of முறை and மறை in lines 3 and 4 is the verse's own chime.

items.claim: guarding sugarcane that has no fence is painful
living under an old roof through which the rain drips is painful
a kingship that rules without justice is painful
a deed carried out without secrecy is painful

6.reading: The verse counts four painful things: harsh words even from those of virtuous mind, men of martial mind slackening in battle, the giving of those who are themselves in distress, and the words of the crooked.
6.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are set against each other, அறமனத்தார் and மறமனத்தார்: each failure is the opposite of the person's own nature. The third item counts a gift as a pain when the giver is in trouble, which the verse leaves without reason: the pain may be the giver's, or the gift's poor fruit.

items.claim: harsh words even from the virtuous-minded are painful
men of martial mind slackening in battle is painful
giving by those who are in distress is painful
the words from the mouths of crooked men are painful

7.reading: The verse counts four painful things: a weapon held by one without strength, the beauty of a flower without scent, the boldness of one without clear judgement, and the speech of one who does not know how to reply.
7.nuance: Each item is a thing cut off from what makes it work: the weapon from strength, the flower from scent, daring from conviction (தேற்றம்), speech from the power to answer (மாற்றம்).

items.claim: a weapon in the grip of one without strength is painful
the beauty of a flower that has no scent is painful
the daring of one who lacks clear conviction is painful
the speech of one who cannot give a reply is painful

8.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the lack of good nature in those whose hearts seem as clear as day, the lack of real affection in friends made in laughter, the flight of those who rose up in hostility, and the friendship of the ungracious-minded.
8.nuance: Three of the four items are about friendship and its counterfeits. பகல் போலும் நெஞ்சத்தார் can mean hearts open as daylight or hearts even as the balance (பகல், the middle); either way the pain is a fair appearance with no character behind it. நார் is the fibre of affection that binds.

items.claim: the want of good nature in those whose hearts appear as clear as day is painful
the want of binding affection in friends made in laughter is painful
the running away of those who rose up in hostility is painful
friendship with the ungracious-minded is painful

9.reading: The verse counts four painful things: an old town without toddy to the drinkers, the absence of generous patrons to those who seek gifts (named first among pains), the beauty of the ungenerous, and the gait of a horse without harness.
9.nuance: The first two items name their sufferers in the dative (களிகட்கு, பரிசிலர்க்கு), and set the drinker's want of toddy beside the bard's want of a patron, perhaps with irony. முன் gives the bard's lack the first rank; the third item then turns to the ungenerous rich, whose looks are no comfort.

items.claim: an old town without toddy is very painful to drinkers
the absence of generous patrons is painful to gift-seekers before all else
the beauty of those without generosity is painful
the running of a horse that is not harnessed is painful

10.reading: The verse counts four painful things: reciting a song where there is no one who grasps its meaning, going alone down a narrow path dense with darkness, going to those who have no grace, and attempting liberality when one has no wealth.
10.nuance: பொருள் closes the first and last lines: a song without hearers who understand its meaning, generosity without the means. The verse thus sets the wasted gift of words beside the impossible gift of goods.

items.claim: reciting a song where no one grasps its meaning is painful
going alone down a narrow path thick with darkness is painful
going to those who have no grace is painful
attempting liberality when one has no wealth is painful

11.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the shoulders of a wife who is not of one mind with her husband, friendship bound with petty men who have no room in them, association with the intemperate, and coming where one's creditors can see one.
11.nuance: The first item places the pain in the embrace itself (தோள்): physical closeness without agreement (உடம்பாடு). The last is shame rather than danger: the debtor's pain is being seen.

items.claim: the embrace of a wife who is not of one mind is painful
friendship tied with petty men who have no room in them is painful
association with the intemperate is painful
entering where one's creditors will see one is painful

12.reading: The verse counts four painful things: crossing the wasteland at the risk of one's head, the pride of one who lives by carrying a net, living with one's mind set on புலை, which is painful to life, and the desire for womanhood of one who has no breasts.
12.nuance: The second item denies pride to a man who eats by carrying the net, an occupation tied to birth groups in this period, so it ranks people by work. புலை in line 3 may be flesh (as in புலால்) or baseness, or the outcaste; the verse does not fix it. The fourth item is a gender norm whose subject is unclear: a breastless woman longing to be counted a woman, or a man's desire for her; இள்ளாள் is likely a misprint for இல்லாள்.

items.claim: crossing the wasteland with one's head as the forfeit is painful
the pride of one who lives by carrying a net is counted painful
living with the mind set on புலை is painful to life
the longing for womanhood of one without breasts is counted painful

norm.note: a period ranking that denies pride to a netting occupation, and a norm that ties womanhood to the body

13.reading: The verse counts four painful things: a king riding an elephant without a bell, boldness spoken by those without courage, submission to kings who will not bend, and a house where people like a disease live.
13.domain_note: the king and those who serve him
13.nuance: The bell on the war elephant announces the king; without it his progress is unheralded or unsafe. The third item is the courtier's pain: bowing to kings who give no regard in return.

items.claim: a king riding an elephant without a bell is painful
boasts of valour spoken by those without courage are painful
submitting to kings who will not bend is painful
a house where people like a disease live is painful

14.reading: The verse counts four painful things: being deceived by women with curling five-plaited hair, the fallen fruit of a mango hung with clusters, parting from one who is like a joined doll, and the moment when those who should understand do not understand.
14.nuance: Three of the items come from love: the deceit of women (a gendered claim of the period), the parting from a beloved, and the failure of understanding between those who should know each other's minds. The fallen fruit sits among them as an image of sweetness spoiled by its fall.

items.claim: being deceived by women with curling five-plaited hair is painful
the fallen fruit of a mango hung with clusters is painful
parting from one who is like a joined doll is painful
the moment when those who should understand fail to understand is painful

norm.note: a period claim that women deceive, stated as one of the pains of love

15.reading: The verse counts four painful things: riding a poor horse without a bell, the purpose of an undertaking explained by the unlearned, the fine wishes of those who have nothing, and being shamed among many people.
15.nuance: The second item is counsel on an undertaking (கருமப் பொருள்) when the counsellor is unlearned; Iniyavai Narpathu 32 uses the same phrase for counsel given by those who know. புல்லார் புரவி may be a horse of the base or a grass-fed nag.

items.claim: riding a poor horse without a bell is painful
the purpose of an undertaking as the unlearned explain it is painful
the good wishes of those who have nothing are painful
being put to shame among many is painful

16.reading: The verse counts four painful things: storing great wealth without enjoying it, union with enemies who should not be approached, the good looks of a man without eyes, and accounts kept by one who does not know numbers.
16.nuance: The last two items are paired: a handsome man without eyes and an innumerate man doing accounts are both the same lack of sight, one bodily and one learned.

items.claim: storing great wealth without enjoying it is painful
union with enemies who should not be approached is very painful
the good looks of a man without eyes are painful
accounts kept by one who does not know numbers are painful

17.reading: The verse counts four painful things: a fool entering among the worthy who are full and self-subdued, going about when it has grown dark and dim (very painful), the penance of those who do not live subdued by endurance, and abandoning the mother who bore one without caring for her.
17.nuance: ஆன்றவித்த and நோன்றவிந்து echo each other: the worthy are those who have subdued themselves, and a penance without that subduing is a pain. The last item is the one duty in the verse; the rest are misplacements.

items.claim: a fool entering among the full and self-subdued worthy is painful
going about when it has grown dark is very painful
the penance of those who do not live subdued by endurance is painful
abandoning the mother who bore one without caring for her is painful

18.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the mind of a strong man lying idle, facing the chest of one who has valiant warriors, going through the hard forest of the wasteland, and association with the poor in mind.
18.nuance: The first item imagines strength (உரன்) present and the mind (உள்ளம்) asleep, a strong man whose power goes unused. மனவறியாளர் are those empty of mind; the variant அகம்வறியாளர் says the same.

items.claim: the mind of a strong man lying idle is painful
facing the chest of one who commands valiant warriors is painful
going through the hard forest of the wasteland is painful
association with the empty-minded is painful

19.reading: The verse counts four painful things: lack of learning in one born to a good family, good seed sown in the ground failing to sprout, women of good quality lacking modesty, and union where there is no family standing.
19.nuance: குலம் frames the verse: the first and last items are about it. The good seed that does not sprout is the image of the first item, birth without learning. கலத்தல் குலமில் வழி makes union (perhaps marriage, perhaps any mixing) outside family rank a pain, a birth norm. நலத்தகையார் are most likely women, and their lack of நாண் is a gender norm.

items.claim: lack of learning in one born to a good family is painful
good seed sown in the ground failing to sprout is painful
women of good quality lacking modesty is counted painful
union where there is no family standing is counted painful

norm.note: a period norm against union outside family rank, beside a norm of women's modesty

20.reading: The verse counts four painful things: the koel's voice calling in the rainy season, harsh words spoken by those without valour, the failure of the rain's plenty to a town, and ploughing with a sluggish ox.
20.nuance: மாரி opens lines 1 and 3: the koel's song out of season and the rain that fails in season. The verse moves from the unseasonable to the town's want and ends in the field, with the ox.

items.claim: the koel's voice calling in the rainy season is painful
harsh speech from those without valour is painful
the failure of the rain's plenty is painful to a town
ploughing with a sluggish ox is painful

links.note: Acharakkovai 6 lists the dog among things a person in எச்சில் does not look at; Innaa 2 counts a fowl and a dog entering a brahmin's house as painful.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show the dog as a standing source of pollution in the period's code, kept from the eye of the impure person in one book and from the threshold of the brahmin house in the other.

links.note: Pattinathar says not to talk of எச்சில் and of fit and unfit, since people do not know where the impurity lies; Innaa 2 counts animals entering a brahmin's house as a pain, on the reading that the pain is ritual defilement.
links.teaches: The Innaa locates defilement in what crosses a brahmin's threshold, while Pattinathar denies that impurity sits in outward things at all, so the pair shows the purity code and its later Siddha rejection.

links.note: Iniyavai 32 names not living under a king without care for his people as foremost sweet; Innaa 3 names living under fierce kings of bent sceptre as painful.
links.teaches: The two books say the same thing from both sides, and the Iniyavai adds that the sweet thing is a choice (not to live there), while the Innaa's float image shows the subject who has no such choice.

links.note: Kural 557 likens a king's want of kindness to the earth's want of rain; Innaa 3 sets living under a cruel king beside swimming long water without a float.
links.teaches: The couplet measures a cruel king by what the land loses; the Innaa measures him by the subject's helplessness, a swimmer with nothing to hold, which turns the public loss into a private danger.
links.list_adds: It puts life under a cruel king beside the floatless swimmer and the harsh speaker's company, so tyranny is counted among the dangers a person meets rather than among the faults of a ruler.

links.note: Kural 861 says to avoid opposing the strong and to favour enmity with the weak; Innaa 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful, and provoking the fortunate as well.
links.teaches: The Innaa keeps the couplet's first half and drops its second: the danger of opposing the strong stands without the counsel to turn on the weak, and it is widened to those who merely have fortune.
links.list_adds: It sets the harm done to the strong beside the ox-less farmer and the fleeing soldier, so the act is counted as self-inflicted loss rather than weighed as strategy.

links.note: Kural 663 says the strength of a deed is that it is revealed only at its end, and that it brings trouble if it comes out midway; Innaa 5 counts a deed done without secrecy (மறை) as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet explains when secrecy matters (until the end), and the Innaa supplies the images for an exposed undertaking: unfenced cane and a leaking roof.
links.list_adds: It pairs the open deed with rule without justice and gives both two images of unguarded keeping, so secrecy is grouped with protection rather than with cunning.

links.note: Kural 548 says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes of himself; Innaa 5 counts a kingship that rules without முறை as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet looks at the unjust ruler's own fall, while the Innaa, by placing him beside a cane field with no fence, looks at what his subjects suffer while he still rules.
links.list_adds: It makes injustice one of four unprotected things, so the verse judges rule by the protection it fails to give rather than by the king's fate.

links.note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in giving even when they have no means; Innaa 6 counts giving by those in distress as painful, on the reading that இன்னா marks a thing to be avoided.
links.teaches: On that reading the books disagree about the poor man's gift: the Kural praises it as a mark of discernment, and the Innaa ranks it with a warrior idle in battle and a crooked man's word.
links.list_adds: It sets the distressed giver's gift beside the virtuous man's harsh word, so the verse names gifts and words that go wrong because the giver is in the wrong state, not because he lacks virtue.

links.note: Kural 727 likens the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in a பேடி's hand among enemies; Innaa 7 counts a weapon held by one without strength as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet uses the powerless swordsman as a simile for useless learning, and the Innaa counts him plainly but puts beside him the speaker who cannot reply, so the verse holds both halves of the couplet's comparison as separate items.
links.list_adds: It lists the weak man's weapon and the speaker who cannot answer as two items of one kind, where the couplet joins them only as image and subject.

links.note: Kural 650 likens those who cannot expound what they have learned to flowers in bloom without scent; Innaa 7 counts the beauty of a scentless flower as painful.
links.teaches: The Innaa places the scentless flower directly beside the speech of one who cannot reply, which is the Kural's comparison spelled out as two counted pains.
links.list_adds: It turns the Kural's simile into two items, a scentless flower and a speaker who cannot answer, and adds weapon and daring as two more things without their ground.

links.note: Kural 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for rebuking when one oversteps; Innaa 8 counts the lack of binding affection (நார்) in friends made in laughter as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet says what friendship is for, and the Innaa names the pain of the friendship that was only laughter: it has no fibre when it is tested.
links.list_adds: It sets the laughing friend beside the fair-seeming heart without character and the ungracious friend, so the verse ranks three counterfeits of friendship together.

links.note: Innaa 9 counts the absence of patrons as the foremost pain of gift-seekers; in Puram 375 a drummer finds no patron but Ay and wishes that, with Ay gone, there be no patrons at all, lest bards praise kings of worthless wealth.
links.teaches: The bard in the Puram poem prefers the very lack the Innaa ranks first among his pains to service under the ungenerous, which the Innaa counts as a separate pain in its third item.

links.note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's circle to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Innaa 10 counts reciting a song where no one grasps its meaning as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, and the Innaa, by setting the song beside the poor man's generosity, shows it as a gift wasted on both sides: the giver of words has no receiver, the would-be giver of goods has nothing.
links.list_adds: It sets the wasted recital beside a lonely dark path and the penniless man's liberality, so the song without listeners is counted among gifts that cannot arrive.

links.note: Iniyavai 22 names giving with knowledge of one's income as sweet; Innaa 10 names liberality attempted by those without wealth as painful.
links.teaches: The two books say the same thing from two sides, and together they make the measure explicit: giving is judged against income, sweet when it fits and painful when it outruns it.

links.note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) to living with a snake in a hut; Innaa 11 counts the embrace of a wife without உடம்பாடு as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves 'those not in accord' open, and the Innaa narrows the same word to the wife, placing the discord at the closest point of the house, the embrace itself.
links.list_adds: It sets the discordant wife beside the petty friend, the intemperate companion and the creditor's eye, so marriage is counted among the bonds that can turn to pain.

links.note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to living with a snake in a hut; Innaa 13 counts a house where people like a disease live as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet's image is sudden danger and the Innaa's is slow sickness, so the pair shows two ways a house of the wrong people harms: the bite and the wasting.
links.list_adds: It sets the diseased house among the king's and courtier's pains, so a household trouble is counted beside a bell-less elephant and submission to proud kings.

links.note: Iniyavai 32 names as sweet the purpose of an undertaking (கருமப் பொருள்) as those who know its surroundings explain it; Innaa 15 names the same thing explained by the unlearned as painful.
links.teaches: The same phrase is sweet or painful in the two books depending only on who speaks it, which shows that both make the counsellor's knowledge, not the undertaking, decide its worth.

links.note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters are the two eyes of living beings; Innaa 16 sets the good looks of a man without eyes beside accounts kept by one who does not know numbers.
links.teaches: The Innaa places the literal blind man next to the innumerate one, which makes the Kural's metaphor into two counted pains of one kind: both are blind.
links.list_adds: By putting eyelessness and innumeracy side by side as items 3 and 4, the list enacts the couplet's equation of number with sight without stating it.

links.note: Kural 1001 says one who hoards great wealth and does not eat it is as good as dead; Innaa 16 counts storing great wealth without enjoying it as painful.
links.teaches: The couplet judges the hoarder as already dead, and the Innaa, by setting him beside the handsome blind man, makes him one who owns a good he cannot use.
links.list_adds: It pairs unused wealth with unseeing beauty, so the hoard is grouped with gifts that their owner cannot enjoy rather than with failures of giving.

links.note: Kural 840 likens a fool's entering the assembly of the worthy to putting an unwashed foot on a bed; Innaa 17 counts a fool's entering among the worthy (சான்றோருட் பேதை புகல்) as painful, in nearly the same words.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the image of defilement and the Innaa gives the worthy their mark, ஆன்றவித்த (full and self-subdued), which is what the fool's entry offends.
links.list_adds: It sets the fool's intrusion beside a penance without self-subduing, so both are counted as the unsubdued entering where self-mastery is required.

links.note: Kural 656 says not to do what the worthy condemn even to relieve one's mother's hunger; Innaa 17 counts abandoning the mother who bore one as painful.
links.teaches: The Kural uses the mother's need as the hardest case in which a wrong still may not be done, and the Innaa counts her neglect as a pain in its own right, so together they bound the duty: it is weighty, but it does not license blame.
links.list_adds: It sets the mother's neglect beside a fool among the worthy and a false penance, so care for her is counted among the duties of a person's standing rather than as a test case.

links.note: Iniyavai 34 names not going about at night as foremost sweet; Innaa 17 names going about when it has grown dark as very painful.
links.teaches: The same rule appears from both sides with matching intensifiers (முன் in the Iniyavai, பெரிது in the Innaa), so both books rank night travel above their other items.

links.note: Kural 600 says a man's உரம் is the abundance of his உள்ளம் (inner drive); Innaa 18 counts the உள்ளம் of a man who has உரன் lying idle as painful.
links.teaches: The Kural defines strength as drive, so the two cannot come apart; the Innaa names the case where they do, a strong man whose mind sleeps, and counts it as a pain.
links.list_adds: It sets the idle strong man beside the man who faces a warrior's chest, so lost strength and rash strength are counted together.

links.note: Kural 409 says the unlearned born high are worth less than the learned born low; Innaa 19 counts lack of learning in one born to a good family as painful.
links.teaches: Both make learning the test of birth, but the Kural overturns the ranking while the Innaa keeps it, counting the unlearned noble as a failed seed and union outside family rank as another pain.
links.list_adds: It sets the unlearned noble beside a seed that fails to sprout and a union without family standing, so birth is kept as the frame that learning fulfils, not one it overturns.

links.note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Innaa 19 counts union where there is no family standing as painful, on the reading that குலம் is birth rank.
links.teaches: On that reading the two disagree on whether family rank is a ground of worth: the Kural denies it at birth, and the Innaa makes its absence a reason a union is a pain.
links.list_adds: It places union outside family rank beside the unlearned noble and the immodest woman, so birth, learning and women's conduct are counted as one order of standing.

links.note: Thirikadugam 84 joins people of a long line who lack the excellence of learning to poverty; Innaa 19 counts lack of learning in one born to a good family as painful.
links.teaches: Both books set the unlearned man of good family beside a failed source of growth (the badly made tank inlet, the unsprouting seed), so the two together show a shared image: lineage is a resource that learning must make flow.

links.note: Kural 13 says that if the sky fails, hunger torments the world though it is ringed by water; Innaa 20 counts the failure of the rain's plenty as painful to a town.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks of the world and its hunger, and the Innaa of the town and its plenty, flanked by the koel's ill-timed call and a sluggish ox, so the failure is set in the farmer's season rather than the cosmos.
links.list_adds: It sets failed rain between the out-of-season koel and the weak ox, so drought is counted as one of the farming year's mistimings and lacks.

links.note: Innaa 4 counts the soil's moisture passing unused for ploughmen without oxen; Innaa 20 counts ploughing with a sluggish ox as painful.
links.teaches: The book grades the ploughman's lack across two verses: with no ox the wet season is lost, and with a sluggish ox it is wasted, so the ox decides whether the rain is of use.

source_issues: Verse 0 line 2: Project Madurai's variants பொற்பன வெள்ளியை and மன்றப்பின்னாது; tamilvu has no invocation with this number.
Verse 1 line 3: the variant ஊணின்னாது would reverse the third item ('eating in a brahmin's house is not painful'); the site lacks this verse.
Verse 2 line 3: புநடைவை is likely a corruption of புடைவை; with the variant உடையின்னாது the item would reverse, and its sense cannot be fixed.
Verse 4 line 2: கருவிகண் may be கருவிகள் misprinted.
Verse 5 line 2: உறைசேர் against tamilvu உறை சோர் (leaking); the variant புரைசேர் also noted.
Verse 10 line 1: பொருளணர்வார் is likely a misprint for பொருளுணர்வார்.
Verse 11 line 1: variant மனைவி தொழி லின்னா; line 2 டியர்த்த against tamilvu யாத்த.
Verse 12 line 4: முலையிள்ளாள் is likely a misprint for முலையில்லாள்.
Verse 15 line 3: variant விழைவின்னா; line 4 நாணப் against tamilvu நாணுப்.
Verse 18 line 1: மடிந்திருந்தல் may be a misprint for மடிந்திருத்தல்; line 4 variant அகம்வறியாளர்.
